title: Maximum Path Quality of a Graph

reported.text: Nodes have beauty values; find the path within a time limit of 50 that maximises total beauty, counting a revisited node only once.

sources.passage:
Oracle Health IC3 SDE  | Interview Experience | 7 - 10 years

**Round 1 –** This round covered core Java fundamentals. Questions included the differences between interfaces and abstract classes, dependency injection vs. the factory pattern, and scenarios where the Strategy pattern should be used. I was also asked to write a simple Java program to check whether one string is a subsequence of another. (This went very well)

**Round 2 –** This was a challenging round, and I didn’t perform well. They gave a graph problem where each node had a “beauty” value. The task was to compute the maximum beauty along a path, ensuring that if a node was revisited, its beauty was not counted again. Additionally, the chosen path had to be valid only if it stayed within a maximum time limit of 50. I attempted a DFS-based solution but got confused managing both the beauty accumulation and the time constraint.

**Round 3 –** This round focused on behavioral and conceptual topics. They asked why I want to switch my current firm, an example of a conflict I’ve had with a colleague, and a programming question about determining the execution order of jobs—potentially using multithreading. (this also went good)

**Round 4 –** This round involved introductions, responsibilities in my current role, and reasons for wanting to change firms. It also included a high-level design discussion of my current project, followed by a high-level design exercise for a Covid Vaccination System. (I think in a period of 60 mins asking two HLD question is not appropriate, due to time crunch I was not able to come up with perfect HLD of covid system and also the UI where they asked me to build the HLD diagram I was not that fluent so it also consumed lot of my time. Though this round was not that tough but it seems I didn't do well as per my expectations and of course as per the interviewer too :P)

All these rounds were non-eliminatory, and all four interviews took place over the course of two days, with two interviews each day.
Final status – I’ve been ghosted/rejected.

title: Power-of-2 Substrings in a Huge File

reported.text: Count substrings of a digit string that are powers of 2 when the string is on disk and too large for RAM: chunked reading with boundary overlaps, a hash set of powers, and parallel processing.

**DSA Question:** Longest Increasing Subsequence (LIS)

- I first explained the brute force recursive approach.

- Then I optimized it using DP tabulation (O(n²)).
    
- Finally, I discussed further optimization using binary search with extra space (O(n log n)) and wrote pseudocode in C++.
    

---

## Round 3 – Technical Interview 2

The round started with a conceptual question:
Why do we need Redis when programming languages already have hashmaps?

- I explained that Redis provides persistence, rich data structures, and additional features that go beyond simple in-memory maps.
    

**DSA Questions:**

1. Find the nth node from the back of a linked list – solved using two pointers.

2. Find the Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA) in a binary tree – solved using DFS.
    
3. Find all pairs of numbers whose sum is divisible by 60 – solved using complements and hashing.
    

---

## Round 4 – Technical Interview 3

This was a short round with one question:

**Question:** Count all substrings in a very long string of digits that represent powers of 2. The string was too large to fit in RAM and resided on disk.

**My Approach:**  
I processed the string in chunks, making sure to handle overlaps at chunk boundaries. I precomputed all powers of 2 as strings and stored them in a hash set for fast lookup. Then, I slid a window over each chunk and checked substrings against the set. From a system design perspective, I treated it like a small pipeline: a disk reader loads chunks, a processor extracts and checks substrings, and an aggregator combines counts. Multiple chunks could be processed in parallel to make it scalable...
